title: Groups and symmetry
summary: A group is a set with an associative operation, an identity and inverses. Lagrange's theorem, group actions and orbit counting (Burnside) are the first tools.
why: Symmetry is group theory; Fermat's little theorem is Lagrange's theorem for $(\mathbb Z/p)^\times$.

leads_to.title: Homomorphisms, normal subgroups and quotient groups

title: AM–GM and power means
summary: For non-negative reals the arithmetic mean is at least the geometric mean, with equality when all are equal. More generally the power means $M_p$ increase with $p$.
why: Most competition inequalities reduce to weighted AM–GM after the right substitution.

title: Cauchy–Schwarz, Hölder and rearrangement
summary: $(\sum a_ib_i)^2 \le (\sum a_i^2)(\sum b_i^2)$, its Engel form $\sum a_i^2/b_i \ge (\sum a_i)^2/\sum b_i$, Hölder's generalisation, and the rearrangement inequality for similarly ordered sequences.
why: Cauchy–Schwarz is the inequality of inner-product spaces, used everywhere from Fourier analysis to quantum mechanics.

timeline.title: Cauchy's inequality
timeline.text: $(\sum a_ib_i)^2 \le \sum a_i^2\sum b_i^2$ in his Cours d'analyse; Schwarz proved the integral form in 1888.

title: Convexity, Jensen and majorization
summary: A convex function lies below its chords, so $f(\text{mean}) \le \text{mean of } f$. Tangent-line tricks, Karamata's majorization inequality and smoothing arguments extend this.
key_statements: f\Big(\sum w_ix_i\Big) \le \sum w_i f(x_i)\ \ (f \text{ convex},\ \textstyle\sum w_i = 1)
why: Convexity is the reason optimisation problems have unique answers, from mechanics to machine learning.

timeline.title: Jensen's inequality
timeline.text: Convex functions lie below their chords, in any number of points.

title: Symmetric and polynomial inequalities
summary: Inequalities in symmetric polynomials of a few variables: Schur's inequality, Muirhead, sum-of-squares decompositions and the $uvw$ method that reduces to the case of two equal variables.
why: Deciding when a polynomial is a sum of squares is Hilbert's 17th problem, solved by Artin in 1927.

title: Functional equations over the reals
summary: Find all $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ with an identity such as $f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)$. The moves are substitutions, proving injectivity or surjectivity, and pinning down $f$ on rationals before using a regularity condition.
why: Without a regularity condition Cauchy's equation has wild solutions built from a Hamel basis, an early use of the axiom of choice.

title: Polynomials, roots and Vieta's formulas
summary: A degree-$n$ polynomial has at most $n$ roots; its coefficients are the elementary symmetric functions of the roots. Interpolation, the factor theorem and comparing coefficients solve most problems.
why: Polynomials are the objects of algebraic geometry and the workhorse of the polynomial method in combinatorics.
